section.title: Praise the Lord, All Nations
section.sectionRationale: The shortest chapter in the entire Bible, this Hallel psalm packs a universal missionary vision into two verses, summoning every nation and people to praise the LORD, a summons Paul quotes to defend the inclusion of the Gentiles.
section.thesis: God's covenant love toward Israel is the very ground on which every nation on earth is summoned to praise Him, because His faithfulness was never meant to stay within one people's borders.
section.frameNote: A single, tightly compressed movement in two verses: a universal call to praise, verse 1, grounded in the greatness of God's loving devotion and the eternity of His faithfulness, verse 2.

units.label: Praise the LORD, all you nations
units.note: the shortest chapter, the widest summons

verses.text: Praise the LORD, all you nations! Extol Him, all you peoples!
For great is His {{chesed|loving devotion}} toward us, and the faithfulness of the LORD endures forever. Hallelujah!

chesed.gloss: Steadfast, covenant love and loyalty. That this love shown specifically toward Israel, 'us,' verse 2, becomes the stated reason for all nations to praise God shows His covenant faithfulness was always intended to overflow to the whole world.

basic.context: In just two verses, the shortest chapter in Scripture, this psalm summons every nation and people on earth to praise the LORD, grounding that universal call in His steadfast covenant love and enduring faithfulness shown specifically to Israel.
basic.hermeneutics: The psalm's brevity does not limit its scope; rather, its compressed form intensifies a sweeping missionary vision that Paul later reads as proof that God always intended the Gentiles to join Israel in praising Him, Romans 15:11.
basic.originalLanguages: The basis for universal praise is God's chesed, His steadfast covenant love, shown toward 'us,' meaning Israel, verse 2. That love shown to one people becomes, in this psalm's own logic, the reason all peoples everywhere are summoned to praise Him.
basic.typology: This psalm's summons anticipates the promise to Abraham that in his offspring all the families of the earth would be blessed, Genesis 12:3, a promise fulfilled when the ultimate offspring of Abraham, Christ, becomes a light to the Gentiles as well as the glory of His people Israel, Luke 2:32.
basic.christ: Paul quotes this psalm directly in Romans 15:11 as part of his argument that Christ's coming was always intended to bring the Gentiles to glorify God for His mercy, alongside Israel. The chesed shown to Israel that grounds this psalm's universal call is fulfilled in Christ, the offspring of Abraham, through whom God's covenant faithfulness reaches every nation and people exactly as this two-verse psalm anticipates.
basic.god: God's covenant love is not tribal or exclusive in its ultimate purpose; it is shown concretely to Israel yet is so great and so enduring that it becomes grounds for summoning literally every nation and people on earth to praise Him.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 12:3 promises that all the families of the earth will be blessed through Abraham's offspring. Romans 15:11 quotes this psalm directly to defend the full inclusion of Gentile believers in praising God. Revelation 7:9-10 pictures the psalm's summons finally and fully answered, a great multitude from every nation praising God and the Lamb.
basic.oneStory: God's steadfast love shown to Israel was never meant to remain within one people's borders; this brief but sweeping psalm summons every nation to praise Him on that very basis, a summons Paul reads as fulfilled in Christ, through whom God's covenant faithfulness at last reaches, and will finally be answered by, every nation and every people on earth.

context.literary:
Psalm 117 is a hymn reduced to its skeleton. Almost every hymn in the Psalter has three parts, a summons to praise, the reasons for it introduced by 'for,' and a closing call, and here all three fit into two verses. Verse 1 holds two imperatives in parallel, 'Praise' and 'Extol,' each with its own audience, 'all you nations' and 'all you peoples.' Verse 2 begins with the small word 'for' and gives the ground, and then ends with the call to praise again in the single word Hallelujah.

The frame is deliberate. The psalm begins with a command to praise and ends with a word that means the same thing joined to the short form of the divine name, so the whole poem is praise from edge to edge.

A pattern of widening runs across the neighbouring psalms. In Psalm 116 the singer paid his vows before 'all His people,' verse 18. Psalm 117 steps up from 'all His people' to 'all you nations.' Then Psalm 118 returns to a smaller circle, Israel, the house of Aaron and those who fear the LORD, each told to say that His loving devotion endures for ever, Psalm 118:1-4. The Hallel thus breathes in and out, from the rescued individual to the people of God, to the nations, and back to the congregation.

There is also an answer to Psalm 115. There the nations jeered, 'Where is their God?', Psalm 115:2. Here the same nations are told to praise Him. The taunt and the summons stand two psalms apart, and the Hallel's story is of a rescue so plain that the mockers are invited to join the song.

One feature stands out in the reasons. The first person plural, 'us,' appears only in verse 2. The nations are called to praise on the basis of what happened to someone else, and the psalm trusts that the testimony of that people is evidence enough.
context.historical:
Nothing in the psalm fixes its date, and the sensible course is to say only that it was sung in the temple worship of Israel and gathered into the Hallel used at the pilgrim festivals. What can be recovered is the world into which it spoke. In the ancient Near East every people had its own gods, and a nation's fortunes were taken as a verdict on its deity. A small people in the hill country of Judah, repeatedly overrun by empires, would on that logic have a weak god. Psalm 117 makes a bolder claim: this God is the one the whole world should praise.

The claim was not invented in the psalm. Israel's story had always had foreigners in it. At the first Passover a mixed multitude went up with the Israelites, Exodus 12:38, and the law allowed a resident foreigner to keep the Passover if he accepted the covenant sign, Exodus 12:48-49. Solomon's prayer at the dedication of the temple asks God to hear the foreigner who comes from a distant land because of His name, 1 Kings 8:41-43, so that all the peoples of the earth might know Him. The psalm gives that hope a hymn.

Later Israel's contact with the nations was often hard: conquest, exile, dispersion. In those centuries the psalm would have been sung by a people who lived among the peoples it addresses, in Babylon or later in the cities of the Mediterranean world, where Gentile neighbours and God-fearers met Jewish worship. Some in the audience could hear it as an invitation to join, and others as a prayer that the nations would one day.

The words 'loving devotion' and 'faithfulness' were also known as a pair in Israel's creed, going back to the Lord's proclamation of His own name to Moses, Exodus 34:6. The psalm takes that private covenant description and holds it out to the world.
context.canonical:
The psalm draws its logic from Genesis 12:2-3, where Abraham is blessed so that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him. The Lord's covenant love to one family is the channel of blessing to all, and Psalm 117 sings the second half of that promise. It has many companions in the Psalter. Psalm 67:3-4 prays that the peoples will praise God and the nations be glad, Psalm 86:9 says that all the nations He has made will come and bow before Him, Psalm 96:3 tells Israel to declare His glory among the nations, and Psalm 22:27 says that all the families of the nations will bow down.

The prophets take the same line. Isaiah 2:2-3 sees all nations streaming to the mountain of the LORD's house, Isaiah 49:6 makes the Servant a light for the nations, Isaiah 56:6-7 promises foreigners joy in a house of prayer for all peoples, and Isaiah 19:24-25 names Egypt and Assyria alongside Israel as the Lord's people. Malachi 1:11 says that His name will be great among the nations from the rising of the sun to its setting. Zechariah 8:22-23 sees many peoples seeking the Lord in Jerusalem.

The New Testament's use is concentrated in Romans 15:8-12, where Paul strings four quotations together to show that the Gentiles' praise was always in Scripture. He quotes Psalm 18:49, Deuteronomy 32:43, Psalm 117:1 and Isaiah 11:10, which together cover the Psalms, the Law and the Prophets. The other main passages are Acts 15:14-17, where James hears the words of the prophets in the Gentile conversions, and Revelation 7:9-10 and 15:4, where the nations at last come to worship.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalmist wanted Israel to see its own history as a message for the world. The people had received the Lord's covenant love, and that love was not a private possession. It was proof that could be offered to anyone, and the right response of outsiders was praise. For the first hearers this was both a comfort and a charge. It was a comfort because their small, battered nation was not forgotten by a God who intended to be known everywhere. It was a charge because their life as the Lord's people was now a public witness: what the nations saw of Israel was meant to lead them to the Lord.

He also meant to say something about the Lord's character. The word chosen to describe what He had done for Israel, 'great' or prevailing, suggests a love that overpowers and spills over. A God whose commitment to one people could be summed up as faithfulness that lasts for ever is a God of whom it can be said that all peoples have reason to rejoice.

The brevity itself is a message. The psalm does not argue or explain, and it does not threaten the nations with judgment. It simply calls them, with the confidence of a people that has found the good thing and wants others to share it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm is a summons, and a summons is not a report. It does not say that the nations were praising when it was written, nor does it say that every nation will respond. It prescribes praise as the fitting response to the Lord's loving devotion, and it presents the invitation as open to everyone.

It would be a misreading to hear in it a boast of national superiority. The 'us' of verse 2 is the voice of those who received mercy, and the logic of the verse is that what they have received is a ground of praise for others, not a privilege to be guarded. Paul reads it this way in Romans 15:9, where the Gentiles glorify God 'for His mercy.'

Nor should the psalm be turned into a promise that all individuals will be saved without response. The text calls and gives a reason, and the call must be heard. In the New Testament it is acted on through preaching, as Paul argues in the same letter.

What carries forward is practical. Believers are meant to be a people whose praise is audible beyond their own walls. A church that treats worship only as an inward comfort has missed the point of a psalm that tells the nations to join in. At the same time, the call to praise is not a call to impose one's culture. The nations are invited as nations and peoples, and the New Testament upholds that, Revelation 7:9.

debates.question: Are the nations called to join Israel's worship, or simply to acknowledge the Lord?

views.label: A call to be gathered into Israel's worship
views.case: Isaiah 56:6-7 promises that foreigners who join themselves to the Lord will be brought to His holy mountain and made joyful in His house of prayer, and Zechariah 8:22-23 sees people of every tongue seeking the Lord in Jerusalem. On this view Psalm 117 invites outsiders to come to the temple and take their place in the praise of the covenant people.

views.label: A call to recognise the Lord's rule from where they are
views.case: The hymns of Psalms 96 to 100 summon all the earth to praise the Lord as King without implying that everyone must travel to Jerusalem. Psalm 100:1 says 'all the earth,' and Malachi 1:11 pictures worship offered in every place. The psalm may therefore be a universal acknowledgement of His rule and goodness.

views.label: Gentiles praising as Gentiles, with Israel
views.case: Paul's use in Romans 15:9-12 suggests that the nations are to rejoice with God's people and not to become Israel. 'Rejoice, O Gentiles, with His people' is the pattern, and Acts 15 settles that Gentile believers are not required to become Jews. The praise is joint, and the differences remain.

debates.bearing: The first reading emphasises the centrality of Zion, the second the Lord's universal kingship, and the third the shape the New Testament gives to both. What all agree on is that the Lord's covenant love is the reason for the nations' praise, and that no people is shut out of the invitation.

debates.question: Does Paul's use of the psalm in Romans 15:11 fit its original meaning?

views.label: Yes, the psalm already looked for Gentile praise
views.case: The psalm addresses the nations directly and gives a ground for them to praise. Paul does not twist this into something new but says that it is now happening. Romans 15:9-12 simply collects texts from the Law, Prophets and Psalms that say as much.

views.label: Paul brings out a fuller sense in the light of Christ
views.case: The original singer did not know how the nations would come to praise. Paul answers that Christ became a servant to the circumcised for the sake of God's truth, to confirm the promises, so that the Gentiles might glorify God for His mercy, Romans 15:8-9. The words 'truth' and 'mercy' line up with the faithfulness and loving devotion of the psalm, and give the scene a concrete shape.

views.label: The psalm first imagined nations admiring Israel's vindication
views.case: Some see the original expectation as a day when the nations acknowledge the Lord after seeing what He had done for Israel, an event more like witness than conversion. Paul then reads it as being worked out in the church.

debates.bearing: All three recognise that the psalm's direction is toward the nations. Paul's reading is therefore an extension that follows the grain of the psalm and not a reversal of it.

study.originalLanguages:
The two imperatives in verse 1 are addressed to two different groups. 'Praise' is the plural command that gives the whole Hallel its name, and 'Extol' is a second verb for speaking well of God aloud. 'Nations' is the common word goyim, the regular term for the peoples outside Israel, though Israel herself was promised to become a great goy in Genesis 12:2. 'Peoples' is a rarer, more poetic plural. The Septuagint renders the first as 'Gentiles,' ethne, and the second as 'peoples,' laoi, and Paul follows it in Romans 15:11. The plural laoi is worth a note, because the ordinary Greek word laos in the Old Testament usually means Israel. The psalm therefore uses the vocabulary of the 'peoples' for those who are not yet God's people.

The key word of verse 2 is gavar. The BSB renders it 'great,' but the verb means to prevail or be mighty. It describes the waters of the flood that rose and prevailed on the earth in Genesis 7:18-20, and it appears in Psalm 103:11, 'so great is His loving devotion for those who fear Him.' The preposition that follows, 'toward us,' is literally 'over us.' The loving devotion of the Lord has not trickled but has risen and covered, as the flood once covered the land.

'Loving devotion' is chesed, the covenant loyalty that binds God to those whom He has taken, and 'faithfulness' is emet, from the root that gives 'amen,' meaning something firm and dependable. The pair appears first in the Lord's self-description in Exodus 34:6 and then through the Old Testament, for instance Genesis 24:27, Psalm 25:10 and Psalm 85:10. In Psalm 85:10 they are said to meet and be joined together. Here the words stand at the point where Israel's private confession becomes a public argument: because this is who the Lord is, all peoples have reason to praise Him.

'The faithfulness of the LORD' is literally 'the truth of the LORD,' and the verb that follows, translated 'endures,' is not a verb at all in the Hebrew. The line says simply 'and the truth of the LORD, for ever.' The sentence lacks a verb, which makes it read like a plain statement.

The closing word is Hallelujah, a plural command, 'praise,' joined to Yah, the short form of the divine name. It repeats the opening verb, so the psalm's first and last words are the same call, and the name of God sits at the end as the object. The BSB footnote notes that the word means 'Praise the LORD.'

One small detail about the number: the plural 'us' in verse 2 is the first-person plural of the Hebrew suffix, and it is the only place the psalm uses the first person at all. Everything else is addressed to others.

typology.type: The blessing to all families through Abraham, verse 1 with Genesis 12:3
typology.fulfillment: The promise that Abraham's family would bring blessing to every family on earth is the root of the psalm. Paul says Scripture foresaw that God would justify the Gentiles by faith and announced the gospel beforehand to Abraham, Galatians 3:8, and that Christ redeemed us so that the blessing promised to Abraham would come to the Gentiles, Galatians 3:14. The escalation is from a promise carried by a family to a blessing delivered by the one descendant. The type falls short in that Israel as a nation often failed to be the channel, and the fullness comes in one person.

typology.type: The temple as a house of prayer for all nations, verse 1
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah said that the Lord's house would be called a house of prayer for all the nations, Isaiah 56:7. Jesus quoted that when He cleared the temple, Mark 11:17, defending the space where Gentiles could pray. Paul says Christ has broken down the dividing wall so that Jew and Gentile are one in a single holy temple, Ephesians 2:14-22. The correspondence is that a place meant to welcome the nations becomes a people that does. The type is surpassed because the building is replaced by the body of those joined to Christ.

typology.type: Loving devotion and faithfulness embodied, verse 2
typology.fulfillment: The two words of the Lord's covenant name are carried by John into the Gospel's opening, where the Word became flesh and is 'full of grace and truth,' John 1:14, and grace and truth came through Jesus Christ, John 1:17. Paul likewise sees the pair in Christ's service, truth to confirm the promises and mercy for the nations, Romans 15:8-9. The correspondence is not that the words are identical but that the character they name is now seen in a person. The earlier revelation was real but partial, and the person is its fullest form.

The psalm commands the nations to praise, and the Bible's last vision records their reply. A multitude too large to count, from every nation, tribe, people and tongue, stands before the throne and the Lamb and cries out salvation to God, Revelation 7:9-10. The nations who will walk by the city's light bring their glory into it, Revelation 21:24-26. The invitation becomes a fact. The type falls short only in being a call without a conclusion; what the psalm asks, Revelation reports.

study.christ:
Psalm 117 never names a king or a servant, so its link to Christ is not through a titled figure but through the New Testament's reading of its logic. That reading is concentrated in one passage, Romans 15:8-12, and everything hangs on how Paul puts the pieces together.

Paul says that Christ became a servant of the circumcised 'on behalf of God's truth, to confirm the promises made to the patriarchs, so that the Gentiles may glorify God for His mercy.' The two ends of the sentence correspond to the two halves of Psalm 117:2. God's truth, His faithfulness, is shown in keeping the promises to Israel, and God's mercy, His loving devotion, is shown in reaching the Gentiles. The Greek words are aletheia and eleos, and they are the usual Greek renderings of emet and chesed. Paul does not read Christ into the psalm. He reads the psalm as describing what Christ did.

He then lines up four proofs, one from the Psalms, one from the Law, one from the Psalms again, and one from the Prophets. The third is Psalm 117:1, and the fourth, Isaiah's Root of Jesse who will rule the Gentiles and in whom the Gentiles will hope, Romans 15:12, names the figure in whom all this converges. The psalm's call to the nations thus joins the song of the king who praises the Lord among the nations in Psalm 18:49.

The Gospels supply the pattern. Simeon takes the infant Jesus and calls Him a light for revelation to the Gentiles and glory to His people Israel, Luke 2:32, which is verse 1 and verse 2 side by side. When some Greeks come to the feast and ask to see Jesus, He answers that the hour has come, John 12:20-23, as though the Gentiles' approach marks the moment for the cross. After the resurrection He sends His followers to make disciples of all nations, Matthew 28:19, using the same phrase Paul quotes from the psalm. And the vision of the Lamb who purchased people from every tribe and tongue and people and nation, Revelation 5:9, is what is meant by 'all you peoples.'

There is a quieter link. This psalm sits in the Hallel, and the Gospels say Jesus sang a hymn before He went out to the Mount of Olives, Matthew 26:30. It is probable that these two verses were on His lips, though the text only says 'hymn.' If so, the call to the nations was sung by the one who was about to give His life to make it true.

A word of care. The psalm is not a prophecy with a name, and it should not be pressed into more than it says. The sound conclusion is that Paul and the Gospels see in Christ the means by which the Lord's faithfulness to Israel becomes mercy to the nations, so that the summons of Psalm 117 can be answered.
study.god:
The psalm describes God by the way the nations should respond to Him. He deserves the praise of every people on earth. This is no small claim. It declares that He is not one national deity among many but the one whom all the peoples have reason to extol, and it assumes the truth that the Psalter states elsewhere, that all the nations He has made will come and bow before Him, Psalm 86:9.

The ground of the claim is not power or majesty but chesed and emet. Those two words, loving devotion and faithfulness, are the Lord's own account of Himself when He passed before Moses, Exodus 34:6. The psalm picks the personal and relational qualities rather than the cosmic ones. The nations are told to praise the Lord for what He has been to a particular people, because covenant loyalty is the clearest window into His heart.

The verb of verse 2 gives that loyalty a force. The Lord's loving devotion has prevailed over 'us.' It has overwhelmed a people who did not deserve it, as floodwaters overwhelmed a land. The same strong love is why it can overflow its first recipients. A mercy that was merely sufficient for one family would stay with that family, but a love that prevails goes on to cover others.

There is a held tension between particular and universal. The love shown to 'us' is specific, with a name and a history, and the summons to the peoples is general. The psalm does not resolve it by dissolving Israel into humanity or by confining the Lord to Israel. Genesis 12:3 lays the pattern: He chose one family in order to bless all families. His faithfulness to a few is the means by which He shows His heart to the many.

The last line of the psalm makes the second attribute stand alone, 'the faithfulness of the LORD endures forever.' It is the doctrine that God's word does not lapse with changing circumstances. What He promised to Israel in the past is still valid, and what He promises to the nations is equally sure.

For worship, the lesson is that praise is the proper response to being loved and that it is meant to be shared. A congregation that rejoices in God's faithfulness is invited to say so where others can hear, and to desire that others join. The psalm is short enough to be sung in one breath, and its message is that the Lord who has been faithful to us is worth praising by every people.

crossReferences.note: God promises to make Abraham a great nation and to bless all the families of the earth through him. Psalm 117 sings the second half of that promise, taking the Lord's covenant faithfulness to one family as the reason for the nations to praise.

The Lord's proclamation of His own character includes abounding loving devotion and faithfulness. The two words of Psalm 117:2 are borrowed from this self-description, showing that the psalm is built on the most basic confession Israel had about God.

The nations ask scornfully, 'Where is their God?' Two psalms later the same nations are summoned to praise Him. The Hallel moves from taunt to invitation, which shows how far the Lord's rescue is meant to reach.

All the nations He has made will come and bow before the Lord and glorify His name. It supplies the reason behind Psalm 117's summons, that the nations belong to the Lord by creation and so will one day acknowledge Him.

The next psalm picks up the theme of loving devotion that endures for ever and assigns it to Israel, the house of Aaron and those who fear the LORD in turn. After the nations are called, the circle narrows to the congregation answering.

It was not enough for the Servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, so the Lord makes Him a light for the nations to bring salvation to the ends of the earth. This is the prophetic version of Psalm 117's wide invitation and ties it to a person.

The Lord says His name will be great among the nations from the rising of the sun to its setting, and that pure offerings will be presented in every place. The prophet pictures the same worldwide worship that the psalm commands.

Paul gathers four texts, including Psalm 117:1, to show that the Gentiles' praise was foreseen. He sets truth for the patriarchs beside mercy for the Gentiles, mirroring the psalm's two attributes, and ends with the Root of Jesse as the hope of the nations.

Simeon holds the infant Jesus and calls Him a light for revelation to the Gentiles and glory to Israel. In one line he states what Psalm 117 sets in two, the nations summoned and the people whose faithfulness grounds the summons.

Gentiles were once separate from Christ, strangers to the covenants and without hope, but have been brought near through His blood. It describes how the people addressed in Psalm 117:1 come to share the loving devotion that was shown to Israel.

The new song says the Lamb purchased people for God by His blood from every tribe and tongue and people and nation. It supplies the means behind the psalm's summons, a redemption wide enough to include those it addresses.

A multitude too large to count, from every nation, tribe, people and tongue, cries out salvation to God and to the Lamb. This is the reply to the command of verse 1, with the same nations and peoples now standing in the song.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's account of the nations opens early. Genesis 10 lists the families that spread from Noah's sons, and Genesis 11 shows them gathered at Babel and scattered into different languages. The rest of the Old Testament is lived against that scattering, and Genesis 12 is the first hint of what God intends to do about it. Abraham is called out of that world with a promise that all families of the earth will be blessed through him. Psalm 117 is a song for the moment when that promise begins to be heard, a people receiving the Lord's loving devotion and turning to the others with an invitation.

Israel's own calling made the same point at Sinai. The whole earth is the Lord's, and Israel was to be a kingdom of priests, Exodus 19:5-6, which means standing between God and the world on the world's behalf. Solomon prayed that foreigners who came because of the Lord's name would find a hearing, so that all the peoples might know Him, 1 Kings 8:41-43, and the prophets promised that the nations would stream to the mountain of the Lord's house, Isaiah 2:2-3. The exile scattered Israel among the very peoples it was meant to bless, and the Servant was promised as a light for the nations, Isaiah 49:6.

The gospel is where the line breaks through. Jesus is the descendant through whom the blessing comes, and Paul reads His whole ministry as the Lord's faithfulness to the fathers and mercy to the Gentiles, Romans 15:8-9. At Pentecost, God-fearing Jews from every nation under heaven were in Jerusalem, Acts 2:5, and heard the works of God in their own languages, a reversal of Babel's scattered tongues. The mission then went outwards, and James could recognise in it the words of the prophets, Acts 15:14-17.

The story ends where the psalm points. The multitude from every nation, tribe, people and tongue stands before the throne and cries out its praise, Revelation 7:9-10, and the nations walk by the light of the city, bringing in the glory and honour of the nations, Revelation 21:24-26. The two verses that once summoned the peoples to praise become the sound of a world that has answered. The faithfulness of the LORD that endures forever was not wasted on a single people; it was the road by which every people could come home.

sermon.title: Everlasting Truth for the Joy of All Peoples
sermon.why: Piper preaches directly on Psalm 117, unpacking who the nations and peoples are, God's purpose that all peoples praise Him, and how the basis of that praise, God's steadfast love and faithfulness toward Israel, leads inevitably to Jesus Christ as the one through whom all nations are blessed.

quiz.q: How many verses does Psalm 117 contain, and what is notable about this?

options.text: Two verses, making it the shortest chapter in the entire Bible.
options.note: Its brevity does not limit its scope; it carries one of Scripture's most sweeping missionary visions.

options.text: Twenty-nine verses, making it one of the longest psalms.
options.note: That verse count describes Psalm 118, not Psalm 117, which is famously the shortest chapter in Scripture.

options.text: Ten verses, matching the length of Psalm 111.
options.note: Psalm 117 has only two verses, far shorter than Psalm 111's ten.

options.text: Seven verses, matching the length of Psalm 110.
options.note: Psalm 117 has only two verses, shorter even than Psalm 110's seven.

quiz.q: Who is summoned to praise the LORD in verse 1?

options.text: All nations and all peoples.
options.note: This universal address extends the call to praise far beyond Israel's own borders.

options.text: Only the priests serving in the temple.
options.note: The summons is explicitly universal, addressing all nations and peoples, not merely priests.

options.text: Only the king and his royal officials.
options.note: The call is addressed to all nations and peoples broadly, not a narrow royal circle.

options.text: Only the descendants of Abraham by blood.
options.note: The summons explicitly extends to all nations, not solely Abraham's physical descendants.

quiz.q: What is given in verse 2 as the reason all nations should praise the LORD?

options.text: His great loving devotion toward us and His faithfulness enduring forever.
options.note: God's covenant love shown to Israel becomes the stated basis for universal praise.

options.text: Israel's military conquest of surrounding nations.
options.note: The reason given is God's loving devotion and faithfulness, not a military conquest.

options.text: The wealth and splendor of Solomon's temple.
options.note: The psalm's reasoning centers on God's character, His love and faithfulness, not temple architecture.

options.text: A treaty signed between Israel and its neighbors.
options.note: The basis given is theological, God's covenant love and faithfulness, not a political treaty.

quiz.q: How does Paul use this psalm in Romans 15:11?

options.text: He quotes it as scriptural proof that God always intended Gentiles to praise Him alongside Israel through Christ.
options.note: This is one of several Old Testament texts Paul cites to defend full Gentile inclusion in the gospel.

options.text: He quotes it to argue against including any Gentiles in the church.
options.note: Paul's use is the opposite; he cites it in defense of full Gentile inclusion.

options.text: He quotes it only in reference to the Roman emperor's authority.
options.note: Paul's application concerns the praise of God by all nations through the gospel, not imperial authority.

options.text: He quotes it to predict a specific future date for Christ's return.
options.note: The quotation supports Gentile inclusion in praising God now, not a chronological prediction.

quiz.q: What promise to Abraham does this psalm's universal summons anticipate?

options.text: That in Abraham's offspring, all the families of the earth would be blessed, Genesis 12:3.
options.note: This Abrahamic promise is the seed anticipation that this psalm's universal call to praise later flowers into.

options.text: That Abraham's descendants would remain a small, isolated people forever.
options.note: The Abrahamic promise explicitly includes blessing for all nations, the opposite of isolation.

options.text: That Abraham would receive great personal wealth alone.
options.note: The relevant promise concerns blessing for all nations, not merely Abraham's personal wealth.

options.text: That Abraham's descendants would conquer all surrounding empires militarily.
options.note: The promise anticipated is one of blessing extended to all nations, not military conquest.

questions: This shortest of all psalms carries one of the widest visions in Scripture, that every nation would praise God. Does the size of your own current prayers and praise match the size of God's actual purposes for the world?

The basis for universal praise is God's covenant love shown specifically to Israel. How does seeing God's faithfulness to one people as the ground for blessing all peoples change the way you think about His faithfulness to you personally?

Paul reads this psalm as proof that God always intended the Gentiles to be included in praising Him through Christ. Where do you need to expand your own vision of who belongs at the table of God's people?

This psalm anticipates a day, pictured in Revelation 7, when a multitude from every nation will praise God together. How might you take one practical step this week toward that vision, whether through prayer, giving, or relationship?

Piper notes that missions is not arrogance but love, calling the nations to the joy they were created for. Who is one person or people group you could pray for this week to know and praise this same God?

translationNotes.note: Peoples renders the Hebrew ummim, a term for distinct ethnic or cultural groups, paired with goyim, nations, together expressing the widest possible scope of humanity, every group however defined.
This verse is quoted directly by Paul in Romans 15:11 in defense of the full inclusion of Gentile believers alongside Jewish believers in praising God through Christ.
Loving devotion renders chesed, God's steadfast covenant love shown concretely to Israel, here presented as the very basis for a universal summons extending far beyond Israel's own borders.
